None are wince-grade in isolation; together they describe a newtype that picked the easy representation (String) over the canonical one ([u8; 32]) and accreted convenience surface (into_inner + From, struct + enum wrapper) instead of picking a single idiom per axis.

Crypto-security supplement (/review-crypto-security) confidence calibration:

Sections in scope for this crate: Section B (side-channel hygiene, partial — only PartialEq matters), Section C (untrusted input at protocol boundaries, primary), Section G (algorithm/parameter choice, trivial — spec-mandated SHA-256, explicit naming, explicit encoding).

Sections N/A: Section A (no key material — SHA-256 of public blob is public), Section D (no randomness consumed), Section E (no persistence), Section F (no logging beyond derived Debug, which prints the public hex string by design).

Time spent: ~25 min total across all seven sections. Sections A/D/E/F were dispositioned to N/A in < 2 min each because there is no code in this crate that could possibly violate them (no keys, no RNG, no IO, no log statements). That is correct disposition, not insufficient review.

Code paths read: full source of digest.rs (387 lines incl. tests), full lib.rs (54 lines), Cargo.toml, PLAN.md, AGENTS.md. Read both production code AND tests end-to-end. Did not read consumer call sites because none exist yet (jmap-base-client wiring is the open follow-up bead JMAP-v9py.13).

Findings filed: 2 (.24 threat-model docs gap, .25 deserialize allocation bound). Both P3. Both complementary to existing primary-review findings (.17, .9, .22) rather than duplicating them — the supplement adds the protocol-boundary security angle that the primary review treated as idiom/docs questions.

Probability missed P0: ~2%. A wire-shape parse-only type with no key material, no randomness, no persistence, and no IO has very little surface for a P0. The remaining 2% covers: unexpected interaction with serde_json's visitor (e.g. UTF-8-related panic on non-ASCII bytes that pass the JSON-string parse but reach from_hex — checked, from_hex operates on bytes so non-ASCII would just fail the ABNF check, not panic), or a clippy-grade panic I didn't spot. Below the 20% threshold; no P1 to schedule a deeper pass.

Probability missed P1: ~5%. Most plausible missed P1: an algorithm-collision angle on SHA-256 itself (chosen by the spec, not this crate, so not in scope) or a subtle byte-vs-character handling bug in from_hex on multi-byte UTF-8 input. Checked the latter: from_hex uses s.as_bytes().len() not s.chars().count(), so a 64-byte string containing one 2-byte UTF-8 sequence is 64 bytes long but the 2-byte sequence's first byte (always 0xC0-0xFD) fails the ABNF check at the position where it appears. Behavior is correct; the position reported is the byte index, which the docs say. No P1 from this angle.

No bikeshedding signal: the two findings filed are real (one is a documented threat-model gap with a concrete attack class; one is a documented memory-DoS posture at a known protocol boundary). Neither is taste-without-engineering-basis. Both reference what goes wrong concretely. Both recommend specific fixes. Both link to existing primary-review findings they complement rather than duplicate.

Stop here. The crypto-security surface of jmap-cid-types is small enough that further passes would be bikeshedding.
